analysis.one_liner: Requires Congress to approve EPA rules before they take effect and voids existing ones.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in six House committees until the Congress ended, with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would flip how federal environmental rules work. Today, an EPA rule takes effect unless Congress passes a law to stop it. Under this bill, most significant EPA rules could not take effect unless both chambers of Congress passed a joint resolution approving them within 70 working days — and if Congress did nothing, the rule simply died. It would also lower the cost threshold that defines a 'major' rule from $100 million to $50 million, count any rule affecting many farms or any carbon-price rule as major, and cancel every existing major EPA rule unless the agency resubmitted it for this new review. Rules the EPA was writing on air quality, climate, and coal during this period would have had to clear an active vote of Congress to survive.
analysis.who_benefits: Industries that bear the costs of EPA regulation — coal, oil and gas, and other polluting businesses — would gain, because any costly rule would die unless Congress affirmatively approved it. Given the difficulty of passing legislation, inaction alone would block rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coal, oil and gas, and regulated polluters

how_it_helps.text: Makes every significant EPA rule require an affirmative vote of Congress to take effect, so doing nothing blocks the rule — the reverse of current law, where rules take effect unless Congress disapproves them [S2][S3].

Lowers the 'major rule' economic threshold from $100 million to $50 million and adds rules affecting a substantial number of agricultural entities or implementing a carbon tax to the list requiring approval [S2][S3].
Terminates all EPA major rules in effect at enactment unless the EPA resubmits each one for congressional review within 180 days, a transition that could wipe out existing air and climate rules [S3].
Gives the President a narrow 90-day exception for rules needed for an imminent health or safety threat, criminal enforcement, national security, or trade agreements [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The public bears the cost of delayed or blocked environmental protection: rules on air quality, greenhouse gases, and pollution affecting farms would need congressional approval, and any rule not approved within 70 session or legislative days automatically fails. People exposed to pollution the rules would have limited bear the health and environmental consequences.
analysis.who_pays_short: People breathing the air rules protect

drawbacks.text: The 70-day clock is a practical trap: Congress routinely passes fewer than 70 days of legislative business per period, so many rules could fail simply because Congress never got to them — approval by inaction is designed to be the norm [S3].

The bill also blocks judicial review of most decisions under this process and shields the approval resolution itself from being treated as new statutory authority, so a court could not review the substance of Congress's choice to block a rule [S3].

A good-faith objection in its favor: EPA rules can impose large compliance costs on businesses and electricity consumers, and the bill would force elected representatives to vote on them publicly, with new required reporting on jobs added or lost — accountability supporters would call that a feature, not a bug [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is drafted so that inaction kills rules: that makes blocking EPA protections the default outcome, and the transition section would void existing major EPA rules outright. Whatever accountability it adds comes at the cost of making baseline air, climate, and farm-pollution safeguards contingent on a Congress that could simply decline to act.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to six House committees and three of their subcommittees, and none of them ever reported it — it died in committee when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Sam Graves of Missouri introduced the bill on July 14, 2015, with no cosponsors [S1][S4].

The Speaker referred it to six committees — Judiciary, Energy and Commerce, Transportation and Infrastructure, Agriculture, Rules, and Budget — a referral pattern that requires coordinated action by all six before the bill can advance [S1][S5].

Within two weeks it was sent to three subcommittees (Water Resources and Environment, Energy and Power, and Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law), and no further action was ever recorded [S5].
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or Senate action appears in the record before the Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: EPA rules then in effect — including the Clean Power Plan-era climate and air rules — remained in force, so the public kept protections the bill would have voided; coal and other regulated industries lost a mechanism that would have let congressional inaction block new rules.

for.name: Rep. Sam Graves
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Stop the EPA Act of 2015 on July 14, 2015.

against.name: House Judiciary, Energy and Commerce, Transportation and Infrastructure, Agriculture, Rules, and Budget Committees
against.role: Committees of referral; none ever reported the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving the bill to die at the end of the 114th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill drew no cosponsors, so the record shows only a Republican sponsor and no recorded opposition or support beyond the referral itself.

industries.note: The bill would have let coal-related EPA rules — including carbon rules — die unless Congress affirmatively approved them, and would void existing major rules. Its gains come at the cost of weaker air and climate standards for everyone else.
Emission and drilling rules exceeding the new $50 million threshold would need congressional approval to take effect, shifting protection of the industry's costs to the default position.

Any EPA rule significantly affecting a substantial number of agricultural entities would be deemed major and require congressional approval, giving farm interests a veto point over pollution and conservation rules; some smaller farm operations might also benefit from reduced compliance burdens, but the mechanism weakens the pollution controls that affect farm communities' own air and water.
All EPA rules with annual economic effects of $50 million or more would face a congressional approval requirement, making regulatory relief the automatic outcome of congressional inaction.
